name of paper: LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable potential in processing long sequences, yet efficiently serving these long-context models remains challenging due to the quadratic computational complexity of attention in the prefilling stage and the large memory footprint of the KV cache in the decoding stage. To address these issues, we introduce LServe, an efficient system that accelerates long-sequence LLM serving via hybrid sparse attention. This method unifies different hardware-friendly, structured sparsity patterns for both prefilling and decoding attention into a single framework, where computations on less important tokens are skipped block-wise. LServe demonstrates the compatibility of static and dynamic sparsity in long-context LLM attention. This design enables multiplicative speedups by combining these optimizations. Specifically, we convert half of the attention heads to nearly free streaming heads in both the prefilling and decoding stages. Additionally, we find that only a constant number of KV pages is required to preserve long-context capabilities, irrespective of context length. We then design a hierarchical KV page selection policy that dynamically prunes KV pages based on query-centric similarity. On average, LServe accelerates LLM prefilling by up to 2.9x and decoding by 1.3-2.1x over vLLM, maintaining long-context accuracy. Code is released at this https URL.

contents.AI: LSERVE: EFFICIENT LONG-SEQUENCE LLM SERVING WITH UNIFIED SPARSE ATTENTION Shang Yang * 1, Junxian Guo * 1 2, Haotian Tang 1, Qinghao Hu 1, Guangxuan Xiao 1, Jiaming Tang 1, Yujun Lin 1, Zhijian Liu 3, Yao Lu 3, and Song Han 1 3 have authored a pioneering approach detailed at https://hanlab.mit.edu/projects/lserve.ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive abilities in handling long sequences, but efficiently serving these models remains a hurdle. This is due to the quadratic computational complexity of attention during the prefilling stage, along with the significant memory requirements of the key-value (KV) cache during decoding. To tackle these challenges, we present LServe, an innovative system that speeds up long-sequence LLM serving by implementing hybrid sparse attention. This approach integrates various hardware-friendly, structured sparsity patterns for both the prefilling and decoding attention into a cohesive framework. In this way, calculations on less crucial tokens are skipped in a block-wise manner. LServe illustrates how static and dynamic sparsity can coexist in long-context LLM attention, providing multiplicative speed gains through these combined optimizations. Specifically, we modify half of the attention heads into almost cost-free streaming heads during both prefilling and decoding stages. Furthermore, we determine that only a fixed number of KV pages are essential to uphold long-context capabilities, regardless of the context’s length. We then devise a hierarchical KV page selection strategy that dynamically trims KV pages based on query-centric similarity. On average, LServe enhances LLM prefilling speeds up to 2.9 times and decoding from 1.3 to 2.1 times compared to vLLM, all while preserving long-context accuracy. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/mit-han-lab/omniserve.1 INTRODUCTION Large Language Models (LLMs) have instigated a dramatic transformation in the realm of artificial intelligence. As the context window lengths expand, LLMs display extraordinary performance across an array of long-sequence applications (such as Gemini Team, Google, 2024), including but not limited to multi-turn conversations, comprehensive analyses of lengthy documents (Zhang et al., 2024b; Goyal & Durrett, 2020; Huang et al., 2021), understanding across multiple modalities (Xue et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024b; Lin et al., 2024a), and code completion tasks (Li et al., 2023; Lozhkov et al., 2024). These applications often necessitate processing hundreds of thousands of context tokens in practical scenarios, posing specific challenges. In particular, the necessity for rapid prefilling-minimizing the time required for the first token-and the substantial demands on decoding due to the large KV caches that such contexts generate, present significant obstacles. Long-sequence LLMs extend beyond merely accommodating extended contexts. contents.human: ing. These advancements are achieved through inferencetime scaling and the generation of extensive chains of thought (Wei et al., 2022). According to Qin et al. (2024), o1’s internal reasoning process can extend to 20k tokens for mathematical problems, making it the first known longgeneration LLM. Contrary to the conventional belief that the prefilling stage dominates runtime in long-sequence LLMs, when Llama-3-8B (Dubey et al., 2024) is run using TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) with 256k input tokens and 20k output tokens (comparable to o1’s reasoning trace length), the prefilling time is 116 seconds, while decoding takes 540 seconds - almost 5× longer. arXiv:2502.14866v1 [cs.CL] 20 Feb 2025 LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention 2 To enhance the efficiency of long-sequence LLMs, it is essential to optimize both the prefilling and decoding stages rather than focusing on just one. Beyond model architectural modifications in the pre-training stage (Ainslie et al., 2023; Brandon et al., 2024), existing acceleration solutions for long-sequence LLMs primarily address efficiency from two angles. The first approach centers on KV cache quantization, where methods such as QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), KIVI (Liu et al., 2024c), and KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024) employ low-bit quantization to reduce memory usage and I/O traffic, potentially increasing generation throughput. However, these quantization techniques do not lower the number of computations performed in the attention loop, resulting in suboptimal generation speeds as sequence lengths grow. The second approach utilizes approximate sparse attention to improve long-sequence LLM performance. For example, StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024) apply static masking mechanisms to reduce attention complexity, though at the expense of accuracy in long-context tasks and irregular KV cache memory layouts. DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024) advances this strategy by pruning attention computations at a coarser granularity using an optimization-based approach. Other methods, such as MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) and Quest (Tang et al., 2024), implement dynamic sparse attention to accelerate either the prefilling or decoding stage. However, these approaches do not reduce KV cache memory consumption and lack a unified framework to address efficiency challenges in both stages simultaneously. To this end, we introduce LServe, an efficient system for serving long-sequence LLMs that leverages hybrid sparse attention. Recognizing that not all tokens hold equal importance, LServe integrates multiple hardware-friendly, structured sparsity patterns into a unified block sparse attention framework (see Figure 4). Block-level sparsity accelerates attention computation by processing the KV history in discrete blocks. By skipping blocks, we directly reduce the number of sequential iterations, resulting in measured speedups during both the prefilling and decoding stages. Building on the unified block sparse attention framework, LServe further illustrates acceleration opportunities from static and dynamic sparsity. For static sparsity, inspired by DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), we modify the attention masks in the original model by converting half of the attention heads into Λ-shaped masks, transforming these attention heads into streaming heads. Additionally, we fuse the computation of streaming and standard attention heads into unified GPU kernels for both the prefilling and decoding stages, translating theoretical computation and memory savings that translate to up to 1.7× measured speedup. For dynamic sparsity, we observe that query-centric sparsity (Tang et al., 2024) allows for nearly lossless KV compression: the required number of KV tokens to maintain long-context capabilities remains constant (e.g., 4096), regardless of context length. To optimize efficiency, we design a hierarchical page selector to identify important KV pages for each query token, reusing the selection results across tokens to reduce page selection overhead by 4×. Our key observation is that static and dynamic sparsity patterns are orthogonal in long-sequence LLMs. By unifying static and dynamic sparsity with KV cache quantization into a single GPU kernel, LServe achieves compounded efficiency benefits from each individual optimization for decoding stage attention. We benchmark LServe across three long-sequence LLMs-Llama-3-8B, Minitron-4B, and Llama-2-7B-at context lengths up to 512k tokens. Compared to stateof-the-art frameworks like vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b), QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b), and DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), LServe accelerates prefilling stage by up to 2.9× and achieves an average of 1.3×-2.1× speedup in the decoding stage. Furthermore, LServe accomplishes these speedups while retaining the long-context capabilities of the original dense, floating-point models, demonstrating that hybrid attention sparsity is a free lunch for long-sequence LLM serving. 2 BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION 2.1 Background LLM Inference. LLMs are transformer-based architectures with stacked identical layers, each containing attention blocks, feed-forward networks (FFN), and normalization components. LLM inference involves two stages: an initial prefilling stage that handles multiple tokens concurrently, followed by auto-regressive decoding stage where only one token will be processed for each request in a decoding step.
contents.AI: Recent advancements in computation have been made through the enhancement of inference-time scaling and the development of expansive chains of thought (Wei et al., 2022). Research by Qin et al. (2024) has shown that the o1 model’s internal reasoning mechanism can extend to an impressive 20,000 tokens when solving mathematical problems, establishing it as the pioneer of long-generation large language models (LLMs). This defies the standard notion that the prefilling phase dominates the computational time in long-sequence LLMs. For instance, when the Llama-3-8B model (Dubey et al., 2024) runs using TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) with 256,000 input tokens and generates an output of 20,000 tokens, akin to the length of o1’s reasoning chain, the time required for prefilling is 116 seconds, whereas decoding needs 540 seconds-nearly five times more.In tackling the efficiency of long-sequence LLMs, both the prefilling and decoding stages require optimization rather than concentrating on a single aspect. Apart from architectural alterations during the pre-training phase (Ainslie et al., 2023; Brandon et al., 2024), current solutions aimed at accelerating long-sequence LLMs focus on two main strategies. The first method involves KV cache quantization, which includes techniques like QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), KIVI (Liu et al., 2024c), and KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024). These techniques employ low-bit quantization to decrease memory demands and IO traffic, thus potentially boosting generation rates. Nevertheless, this does not diminish the volume of calculations performed within the attention loop, resulting in less than optimal speed as the sequence length increases. A second strategy employs approximate sparse attention to enhance performance in long-sequence LLMs. Models such as StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024) use static masking tactics to cut down attention complexity but sacrifice accuracy with long-context computations and cause irregular KV cache memory layouts. DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024) refines this by employe coarser granularity pruning in attention computations through an optimization-based method. Other techniques like MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) and Quest (Tang et al., 2024) utilize dynamic sparse attention to hasten either the prefilling or decoding processes. However, these methods fall short in reducing KV cache memory utilization and lack a comprehensive framework addressing efficiency challenges across both stages simultaneously.To address this, we introduce LServe, an innovative system designed for efficiently managing long-sequence LLMs by using hybrid sparse attention. Recognizing that not all tokens are equally important, LServe integrates multiple hardware-friendly, structured sparsity patterns into a cohesive block sparse attention framework (illustrated in Figure 4). By using block-level sparsity to boost attention computations and handling the KV history in set blocks, we can bypass certain blocks altogether-effectively lowering the number of sequential iterations, and thereby achieving noticeable speed increases in both the prefilling and decoding stages.Building upon the unified block sparse attention framework, LServe further uncovers acceleration opportunities through static and dynamic sparsity. With static sparsity, taking inspiration from DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), we revamp the attention masks from the initial model, converting half into Λ-shaped masks that then become streaming heads. Furthermore, we integrate the processing of both streaming and standard attention heads into unified GPU kernels for prefilling and decoding stages, realizing theoretical computation and memory enhancements that result in speed increases of up to 1.7 times. Regarding dynamic sparsity, our findings show that query-centric sparsity (Tang et al., 2024) permits nearly lossless KV compression, with the count of necessary KV tokens to sustain long-context capabilities remaining unchanged (e.g., 4096), irrespective of the context length. To maximize efficiency, we developed a hierarchical page selector that identifies crucial KV pages for each query token, leveraging these results across tokens to significantly lessen, by a factor of four, the overhead of page selection.A key observation is that static and dynamic sparsity patterns remain orthogonal within long-sequence LLMs. By unifying static and dynamic sparsity alongside KV cache quantization in a single GPU kernel, LServe amalgamates the efficiency benefits of each optimization for attention during the decoding stage. We tested LServe against three long-sequence LLMs-Llama-3-8B, Minitron-4B, and Llama-2-7B-at context lengths reaching up to 512,000 tokens. When compared to leading frameworks like vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b), QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b), and DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), LServe accelerates the prefilling stage by as much as 2.9 times and achieves average speedups in the decoding phase ranging from 1.3 to 2.1 times. Importantly, LServe retains the long-context proficiency of the original dense, floating-point models, illustrating that hybrid attention sparsity offers significant advantages for long-sequence LLM serving.Background and Motivation:LLM inference relies on transformer architectures composed of stacked identical layers, each with attention blocks, feed-forward networks (FFN), and normalization elements. The inference process includes a prefilling stage, dealing with multiple tokens simultaneously, followed by an auto-regressive decoding stage that processes only one token per request within each decoding cycle.

contents.human: In LLM serving, the generation length of each sequence is highly variable and unpredictable. Padding all sequences to the maximum length results in considerable memory waste and fragmentation. To address this, vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b) introduces PagedAttention, a KV cache management algorithm inspired by operating systems’ virtual memory. Instead of allocating a continuous memory buffer for each sequence’s KV cache, PagedAttention partitions the cache into fixed-size blocks (or pages), each holding KV data for a set number of consecutive tokens (typically 16 to 64). A page block table records the physical address of each page, allowing the PagedAttention kernel to use indirect addressing to retrieve KV features. TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) and QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) implement quantized page attention to reduce memory bandwidth usage during the decoding stage, resulting in further generation speedups. 2.2 Motivation Serving long-sequence LLMs is challenging due to the high cost of attention. Figure 2 profiles the latency breakdown of Llama-3-8B with a batch size of 1 across various sequence lengths on the A100 GPU. In both the prefilling and decoding stages, attention kernels account for at least 50% of the runtime at sequence lengths over 64k, rising to 75% at 128k. According to QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), the ratio of attention kernels in end-to-end runtime will increase as the batch size scale up. Therefore, in real-world serving scenarios, optimizing the attention becomes increasingly critical. Accelerating attention in long-sequence LLMs requires a deep understanding of attention kernel implementation on GPUs, as illustrated in Figure 3. In both stages, the computation along the KV token dimension remains sequential. In each iteration, a block (depicted as a grid with an orange contour in Figure 3) is computed collaboratively by all threads in the current thread block. Although skipping certain computation within each block is possible, it yields minimal speedup. This is due to the lockstep execution of threads within a GPU warp, where faster threads are forced to wait for slower ones. That said, rather than focusing on sparsity within each iteration, a more effective way to accelerate attention is to reduce the number of sequential iterations along the KV token dimension. This approach leads to our unified block sparse attention formulation, where attention computation is skipped in a blockwise manner. In this scheme, aside from the most recent KV block, each block is either fully computed or entirely skipped during the prefilling stage. During decoding, each sequence contains only one query token, reducing the dimensionality of each orange-contoured grid to 1×P, where P represents the page size (i.e., the number of KV tokens per page). We will detail LServe’s sparsity pattern selection in Section 3. Additionally, because the decoding stage is memory-bound, KV cache quantization also contributes to speed improvements. Quantization is orthogonal to block sparsity, as it reduces the runtime of each iteration, while sparsity reduces the number of iterations. 3 LSERVE: LONG-SEQUENCE SERVING WITH UNIFIED SPARSE ATTENTION We introduce LServe, an efficient long-sequence LLM serving system featuring sparse attention. LServe integrates various sparsity patterns into a unified framework. sparse attention patterns are unified within a block-sparse formulation (Figure 4), and are flexibly supported through fused CUDA kernels. LServe also supports weight, activation and KV quantization, which significantly improves generation throughput at shorter context lengths. 3.1 Unified Block Sparse Attention As shown in Figure 3, skipping computations in the attention kernel by blockwise processing accelerates execution by shortening the sequential loop. Building on this, we introduce a unified block sparse attention pattern for both the prefilling and decoding stages: each thread block computes a TQ × TK tile (and TK × TV ) in parallel. Here, TQ > 1 in the prefilling stage and TQ = 1 in the decoding stage, with TK (or TV ) corresponding to the page size in PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023a). We define block sparsity in LServe as follows: for each TQ × TK tile in the attention calculation, it is either fully skipped (Figure 4(b), light gray blocks) or retained as in standard causal attention (Figure 4(b), blue blocks). Given that each GPU streaming multiprocessor can execute only a limited number of thread blocks simultaneously, the attention kernel execution time can be approximated by the total count of TQ × TK (and TK × TV ) blocks. With a block sparsity of r, where rN of the N total blocks are empty, the theoretical speedup from block sparse attention is 1/(1 -r). For example in Figure 4(b), 10 out of N=21 blocks are non-empty. Thus, the theoretical speedup ratio is 2.1×. Figure 4(c)(d) shows two sparsity patterns used in LServe. The first is streaming attention (Figure 4(c)), a specialized form of block-sparse attention where each token only attends to its immediate neighbors and initial tokens, known as attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2023). Unlike dense attention, where computation for each row scales with the token index, streaming attention keeps the computation for each token constant-in this case, only two local blocks and one sink block, as shown in Figure 4(c). This pattern is nearly costfree in applications with extremely long contexts. Because streaming attention follows a fixed pattern, we designate which heads use it in offline, and make it static for different input sequences in both prefilling and decoding. The second type of sparsity, illustrated in Figure 4(d), is page sparsity, which is specifically designed for the decoding stage where TQ = 1 applies to both skipped and selected pages. Unlike streaming attention, page sparsity in LServe is dynamic, allowing different query tokens to attend to different KV pages. As noted in Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023), dynamic sparsity results in higher compression ratios than static sparsity. Our observations indicate that static sparsity offers up to a 2× efficiency gain, whereas dynamic sparsity bounds the decoding complexity to a constant, with each query attending only to a fixed number of KV tokens. 3.2 LServe System Overview We present an overview of LServe in Figure 5. Built on QServe, which natively supports quantized LLMs, LServe enhances the baseline system by introducing sparsity into both prefilling and decoding dataflows. The two-way paged KV cache serves as the bridge between these two stages. As discussed in Section 3.1, we statically partition the attention heads of a pretrained LLM into two groups: dense heads and streaming heads. Unlike conventional LLM serving systems, which maintain a single KV cache, we utilize separate KV caches for the dense and streaming heads. The KV cache for the streaming heads is organized similarly to the pages in QServe, with scaling factors and zero points stored immediately after the token features. Additionally, the KV cache for the dense heads includes key statistics that facilitate critical page selection during the decoding stage. In the prefilling stage, the key differences between LServe and conventional dense-attention LLM serving systems are twofold: (1) we replace the dense attention kernel with our unified block sparse attention kernel, and (2) we write back quantized KV features using two distinct kernels. In the decoding stage, our system incorporates dynamic attention sparsity. Rather than developing an entirely new dynamic sparse attention kernel, we decompose the problem into two components: (1) dynamic page selection and (2) a dense attention kernel with shorter page tables, where the shorter page tables are provided by the page selector. Notably, our page selector employs hierarchical paging and reusable page selection, enhancing both long-context accuracy and page selection efficiency. contents.AI: In the context of serving large language models (LLMs), the length of each sequence generation can vary significantly and is often unpredictable. Using padding to extend all sequences to match the longest one leads to inefficient memory usage and significant fragmentation. To tackle this issue, vLLM (as detailed by Kwon et al., 2023b) has introduced PagedAttention, a cache management system for key-value (KV) pairs which is inspired by the principles of virtual memory in operating systems. Rather than assigning a continuous memory buffer for each sequence’s KV cache, PagedAttention divides the cache into fixed-size blocks, also referred to as pages. Each page is designed to store KV data for numerous consecutively processed tokens, usually in the range of 16 to 64. A specific page block table records where each page is stored physically, which allows the PagedAttention kernel to employ indirect addressing techniques for KV data retrieval. To enhance performance further, TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) and QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) apply quantized page attention. This reduces memory bandwidth usage during the decoding process, leading to additional improvements in generation speed.### 2.2 MotivationServing long-sequence LLMs is a complex task primarily due to the substantial costs associated with attention mechanisms. Figure 2 highlights the latency breakdown for the Llama-3-8B model, when processing with a batch size of 1, over varying sequence lengths on the A100 GPU. In both the prefilling and decoding phases, attention kernels are responsible for at least fifty percent of the processing time for sequences exceeding 64k in length, and this usage escalates to seventy-five percent at lengths of 128k. As noted by QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), the proportion of attention-related processing in overall runtime will escalate as the batch size increases. Consequently, optimizing attention is crucial in practical deployment settings. Accelerating attention for long-sequence LLMs necessitates a profound understanding of how attention kernels are implemented on GPUs, as depicted in Figure 3. In the prefilling phase, operations labeled Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, K0, K1, K2, K3, K4, and V0, V1, V2, V3, V4 move towards O0, O1, O2, O3, O4 through computational activities. Dense calculation in this stage takes six time units and runs parallelly for prefilling but sequentially for decoding. Sequential operations on K0, K1, K2, K3, K4 with their respective V blocks transform to smaller units in expanded calculation time-demonstrating a shift to block sparse calculations taking four time units. The illustration in Figure 3 outlines attention computations on GPUs, where, in both the decoding and prefilling phases, each query token navigates all key and value tokens sequentially by block processing. Bypassing KV blocks minimizes sequential iterations, directly boosting attentiveness pace. The attention kernel benefits from parallelization across batch sizes, attention heads, and query tokens, with the number of query tokens limited to one during the decoding phase. Regardless, computation across the KV token dimension persists sequentially. Every cycle collaboratively processes a block, represented as a grid, by all active threads within the existing GPU block. While omitting parts of the computation within each grid unit is feasible, it brings negligible speed increases. This limitation tracks back to how threads execute uniformly within a GPU warp, where faster threads remain idle awaiting slower ones. Beyond increasing iteration sparsity, a more effective boost route for attention is by whittling down the frequency of sequential iterations along the KV token dimension. This leads to a specialized unified sparse attention formulation, skipping attention calculations in a block arrangement. This construction allows retention only of the most up-to-date KV blocks for evaluation. During the decoding phase, every sequence contains a single query token, narrowing the dimensions of each block to 1×P, where P symbolizes the number of KV tokens per page. We elaborate on how LServe selects sparsity patterns in Section 3. Additionally, since the decoding phase encounters memory constraints, quantizing the KV cache is another method for achieving faster processing. Quantization acts as a standalone approach to trimming the time needed for each iteration, operating in tandem with sparsity that curtails how many iterations occur.### 3 LSERVE: LONG-SEQUENCE SERVING WITH UNIFIED SPARSE ATTENTIONLServe presents itself as an efficient system designed to serve long-sequence LLMs by adopting sparse attention mechanisms. By integrating various sparse attention patterns into one framework, illustrated in Figure 4, LServe supports these patterns through combined CUDA kernels. The platform also facilitates weight, activation, and KV quantization, significantly boosting throughput at shorter context lengths.### 3.1 Unified Block Sparse AttentionAs demonstrated in Figure 3, skipping computations within the attention kernel by utilizing blockwise processing dramatically enhances the execution flow by reducing the length of sequential loops. Building upon this optimization, we introduce a unified block sparse attention model effective for both the prefilling and decoding stages: Every thread block computes a TQ × TK tile (and TK × TV half) in parallel, where TQ exceeds 1 during the prefilling stage and equals 1 during the decoding, with TK (or TV) corresponding to page size identified in the PagedAttention approach (Kwon et al., 2023a). We describe block sparsity in LServe through this formalization: Each TQ × TK tile during attention calculation is either skipped entirely or processed similarly to traditional causal attention. Owing to the capacity limits of GPU streaming multiprocessors, only a finite number of thread blocks can execute simultaneously. The total number of TQ × TK (and TK × TV) blocks largely determines the attention kernel’s execution time. Assuming a block sparsity ratio of r, with rN of the N total blocks as empty, the theoretical speedup from adopting block sparse attention is calculated as 1/(1-r). Using the example in Figure 4(b), where 10 out of N=21 blocks contain data, the approximate speedup scales up by 2.1 times. Figures 4(c) and (d) demonstrate two sparsity patterns utilized in LServe. The initial format, referred to as streaming attention (Figure 4(c)), is a unique block-sparse selection where each token is linked only to nearby and initial “sink“ tokens (as described by Xiao et al., 2023). Opposed to dense attention, where the computational demand escalates with the token index, streaming attention stabilizes each token’s workload-typically involving just two local blocks plus one sink block, exemplified in Figure 4(c). This sparse format incurs minimal cost in ultra-long-context applications and keeps a standardized pattern across prefilling and decoding for assigned heads, which remains static for differentiating input sequences. The second sparsity type, depicted in Figure 4(d), termed page sparsity, is specifically tuned for the decoding cycle where TQ equals 1 for all pages. In contrast to streaming attention, page sparsity in LServe shows a dynamic nature, allowing alternate query tokens to engage with different KV pages. As Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023) discusses, dynamic sparsity methods achieve a greater compression ratio in comparison to static models. Data indicates static sparsity can double efficiency, while dynamic sparsity maintains the decoding burden consistently, with each query tapping only into a predefined batch of KV tokens.### 3.2 LServe System OverviewAn illustrative depiction of LServe is presented in Figure 5. By leveraging QServe’s offerings that inherently support quantified LLMs, LServe heightens it by introducing sparse data handling during both prefilling and decoding phases. A dual-purpose paged KV cache acts as a conduit linking the operations across these stages. As emphasized in Section 3.1, attention heads in a pre-trained LLM are categorically assigned into dense and streaming groups. Diverging from standard LLM serving mechanisms maintaining a lone KV cache, our system employs distinct caches for dense and streaming categories. Streaming KV caches mimic the page framework seen in QServe, with scaling metrics and zero indicators accompanying token-specific features closely. For the dense collection, crucial page admission information that guides key selections during decoding is embedded. Notably, during the prefilling stage, LServe diverges from traditional dense-attention LLM setups in two principal areas: (1) replacing the conventional dense attention kernel with the newly unified block sparse variant, and (2) reverting quantized KV features using separate kernels in writing operations. In the decoding scenario, LServe implements dynamic attention sparsity. Rather than crafting an entirely novel dynamic sparse attention concept, the approach decomposes it into integral pieces: dynamic page selection interwoven with a dense attention kernel supported by abbreviated page tables provided by the page selector. Our page selector incorporates hierarchical paging techniques and features reusable strategies that advance the accuracy for extensive contexts and optimize page selection efficacy.

We omit normalization layers and residual connections in this figure for the sake of simplicity. 3.3 Prefilling Stage: Sparsity Determination We adopt the approach from DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024) to classify each attention head as either a retrieval head or a streaming head. Using DuoAttention’s optimization-based identification method, we obtain a gating value α ∈[0, 1] for each head, where values closer to 1 signify a retrieval head, and values closer to 0 indicate a streaming head. To classify a head as a retrieval head, we compare α to a threshold τ, determined by a sparsity quantile. For instance, with a target sparsity of 50% across attention heads, τ equals the median of all gate values, thereby designating half of the heads as retrieval heads. 3.4 Prefilling Stage: Kernel Implementation To effectively translate sparsity into performance gains, it is essential to avoid iterating over a complete sequential loop and relying on conditional statements to determine data loading and computation requirements. This method is inefficient for GPU computation patterns, which thrive on minimizing branching within loops. Instead, we should focus on iterating only over the necessary blocks by accurately calculating offsets to load data and assess whether a block should be processed. To facilitate this, we introduce an iterator-based abstraction that standardizes indexing operations. This allows us to loop exclusively over the blocks requiring computation, with data offsets easily computed using offset = iter(i + 1) -iter(i). This abstraction efficiently skips unnecessary blocks with minimal overhead and necessitates few changes to the kernel function, thus enhancing maintainability. Take the streaming heads as an example, the iterators are determined outside the attention kernel since streaming heads are configured offline and the attention pattern is fixed. Once the attention on sink tokens is complete, the iterator automatically updates the memory pointer to the first local token in the KV cache with minimal overhead. Additionally, our iterator-based formulation unifies the more general block sparse pattern (see Figure 4). 3.5 Decoding Stage: Sparsity Determination To further enhance the long-context LLM decoding throughput, we introduce dynamic sparsity upon the input-agnostic static sparsity in Sec. 3.1. 3.5.1 Challenge: the Page Size Dilemma In the decoding stage, the attention operation is memorybound, so state-of-the-art systems typically implement KV cache quantization to reduce device memory usage and enhance throughput. This flexibility enables some heads to operate with page-level sparsity while others follow the streaming computation pattern. To leverage this, we employ a two-level indexing hierarchy to unify the operations for streaming heads and dense heads with dynamic sparsity. Specifically, the low-level (physical) index corresponds to the iteration step of current GPU thread, which executes in a consecutive manner as in dense attention, while logical index denotes the actual position of the target token within the entire KV cache. For each dense head, the page selector provides an index table to map physical index to logical index. Figure 5 presents an overview of the LServe system. At the prefilling stage, LServe efficiently processes both dense and streaming heads by utilizing a fused sparse attention kernel. The past keys and values are cataloged in two distinct paging systems: one tailored for streaming heads and the other for dense ones. During the decoding phase, LServe uses a method of dynamic sparsity by employing a page selection procedure specifically for dense heads. Only the specified KV Pages are retrieved for attention operations in the decoding step. For clarity, normalization layers and residual connections have been intentionally excluded from this figure.3.3 Prefilling Stage: Determining SparsityFor determining sparsity, we use the approach set forth by DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), classifying every attention head as a retrieval or streaming head. Through DuoAttention’s optimization-based classification technique, we determine a gating value α that lies within [0, 1] for each head. A value proximate to 1 indicates a retrieval head, while one near 0 points to a streaming head. To classify a head as a retrieval head, α is compared against a threshold τ, which is established by a sparsity quantile. For example, achieving a target of 50% sparsity across attention heads results in τ being set as the median of all gate values, thereby designating half of the heads as retrieval heads.3.4 Prefilling Stage: Implementing the KernelTo successfully translate sparsity into performance benefits, it is critical to eschew complete sequential loops and avoid using conditional statements for determining data loading and computation prerequisites. Such methods are not efficient for GPU computations, which perform best when branching within loops is minimized. Instead, our focus should be on iterating solely over necessary blocks while accurately calculating offsets that facilitate data loading and evaluation for processing needs. We deploy an iterator-based abstraction to standardize indexing operations, allowing us to loop exclusively over blocks necessitating computation. Offsets are easily derived using offset = iter(i + 1) - iter(i). This streamlined abstraction allows bypassing unneeded blocks with minimal overhead while requiring only minor alterations to the kernel function, thereby boosting maintainability. In the context of streaming heads, iterators are configured external to the attention kernel since streaming heads are prepared offline and the attention pattern is pre-defined. Following attention to sink tokens, the iterator updates the memory pointer to address the first local token in the KV cache with minimal extra cost. Our iterator-based approach further standardizes the more comprehensive block-sparse pattern, as depicted in Figure 4.3.5 Decoding Stage: Sparsity DeterminationTo further improve the throughput during long-context LLM decoding, we introduce a layer of dynamic sparsity on top of the established static sparsity addressed in Section 3.1.3.5.1 Navigating the Page Size Dilemma in DecodingThe attention operation in the decoding stage is memory-bound, prompting state-of-the-art systems to utilize KV cache quantization to minimize device memory consumption and boost throughput. However, this quantization introduces unique challenges for optimization. Specifically, a decrease in the bit-width of KV tokens mandates bigger page sizes to sustain GPU memory bandwidth utilization. Neglecting this can cause notable throughput losses, as seen in Table 1. The efficient LServe system confronts this predicament; for instance, scaling up KV page sizes can complicate theories like those proposed by Quest (Tang et al., 2024), which predict token criticality with page-level statistics, as illustrated in Figure 6. 3.5.2 Implementing Hierarchical Paging for Balancing Accuracy and EfficiencyFailures in query-aware KV cache selection, as shown in Figure 6, arise not because of the higher granularity of sparse attention (i.e., larger page sizes) but due to the homogenization and reduced representation of page-wise statistical indicators when too many tokens are incorporated within a single page. To counter this, we have developed a straightforward, yet effective hierarchical paging system that installs an abstract layer of virtual logical pages to estimate token criticality while maintaining the original memory configuration of the KV cache in physical pages. This concept is vividly depicted in Figure 7, where tokens are grouped into logical pages and nested within physical pages. In this setup, tokens in the same logical page collaborate on the criticality estimator. Within LServe, the channel-wise minimum and maximum values of keys in a logical page serve as representative vectors-a potent metric for evaluating page importance with a moderate page size (≤16), as corroborated by Tang et al. (2024).3.5.3 Optimizing Sparse Attention Overheads through LocalityOne critical inquiry remains: will the larger physical pages necessitate a higher token budget to preserve sparse attention accuracy? Assuming the essential history tokens distribute within the logical page set P = {P(i, j)} during a generation step, where i and j index the physical and logical pages, respectively. If the distribution is random and sparse, these logical pages may scatter across different physical pages, necessitating selecting all |P| physical pages (comprising |P| × NP tokens) to avoid losing vital data. Yet, by leveraging semantic continuity in natural language, which endows the attention operation with an intrinsic locality, LServe can maintain a consistent sparse attention token budget even for larger physical page sizes. Specifically, during the decoding stage, contextual token coherence leads the current query token to align with adjoining pages in the KV cache. As such, prominent logical pages tend to form clusters within similar physical pages. This spatial locality effectively mitigates the demands for an increased token budget, reducing the overhead linked to contrasting quantization and sparse attention.3.6 Decoding Stage: Implementing the KernelThroughout the decoding stage, attention heads are processed concurrently on the GPU, enabling various sparsity patterns to apply to each head separately. This allows some heads to function with page-level sparsity while others follow the streaming computation pattern. We utilize a two-tier indexing hierarchy to unify operations for both streaming and dense heads with dynamic sparsity. The lower physical index corresponds to the current GPU thread iteration step and executes consecutively as in dense attention. In contrast, the logical index indicates the target token’s definitive position within the entire KV cache. For each dense head, the page selector furnishes an index table connecting the physical index to the logical one, whereas streaming heads are handled as dynamic sparse heads with index tables containing only sink and local pages.Table 2: LMM Serving System Accuracy EvaluationWe assessed accuracy on LongBench (Bai et al., 2023) across two models and ten different benchmarks using our approach against standard dense attention. Models like Llama-3-8B and Llama-2-7B were evaluated, with metrics such as LServe’s comparative performance across benchmarks like 2WikiMQA and DuReader, showing LServe often maintaining or slightly improving average performance. Figure 9 further evaluates accuracy through the Needle-in-a-Haystack metrics.4 Evaluation4.1 Evaluation SetupImplementation: Our implementation of LServe utilizes CUDA and PTX assembly based on the frameworks from QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) and NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM (2023) system. The specialized CUDA kernels are integrated into PyTorch for enhanced flexibility and compatibility with a purely PyTorch-oriented serving interface.

contents.human: Testbed. Our primary experiments are conducted on a server equipped with 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, 2 AMD EPYC 7763 CPUs (128 cores), and 2TB of memory. Unless explicitly stated, all experiments utilize the A100 GPUs. Additionally, we perform some evaluations on a cloud instance with a single NVIDIA L40S 48GB GPU to assess system performance across different GPU architectures. All evaluations use PyTorch 2.5.0 with CUDA 12.4 and cuDNN 9.2.0.
contents.AI: Testbed. The core of our experiments takes place on a high-performance server that is outfitted with a set of 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each possessing 80GB of memory. This server is further augmented by 2 AMD EPYC 7763 processors, offering a substantial total of 128 cores, and is supported by 2TB of RAM. It is important to note that, unless specifically mentioned otherwise, every experiment leverages the capabilities of the A100 GPUs. In addition, to explore system performance across diverse GPU architectures, we conduct several evaluations on a cloud-based instance equipped with a single NVIDIA L40S GPU, featuring 48GB of memory. Throughout all evaluations, we employ PyTorch version 2.5.0, coupled with CUDA version 12.4 and cuDNN version 9.2.0, ensuring consistency and reliability in our testing environment.

contents.human: Models. To comprehensively assess system performance across various LLM architectures, we utilize the widely adopted GQA-based model Llama-3-8B (Dubey et al., 2024), the MHA-based model Llama-2-7B (Touvron et al., 2023), and the smaller-scale model Minitron-4B (Muralidharan et al., 2024). Additionally, to support long-context inference, we employ the context-extended Llama-3-8B version Gradient (Pekelis et al., 2024).
contents.AI: Models. To thoroughly evaluate the performance of systems across a range of large language model (LLM) architectures, we employ several models that are well-regarded in the field. Among these is the highly recognized GQA-based model, Llama-3-8B, as detailed in Dubey et al. (2024). We also make use of the MHA-based model known as Llama-2-7B, which is discussed in the work of Touvron et al. (2023). Alongside these, we include the smaller-scale Minitron-4B model, as researched by Muralidharan et al. (2024). Furthermore, to facilitate inference in scenarios requiring extended contexts, we deploy the context-extended version of Llama-3-8B, which is termed Gradient, as outlined by Pekelis et al. (2024).

contents.AI: Metrics are pivotal in our analysis, with a primary emphasis on improving serving throughput. Specifically focusing on Table 3, which deals with accuracy evaluation on RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024), we scrutinize how Llama-3-8B performs across various RULER benchmarks. These benchmarks pose significant challenges, including tasks like multi-hop tracing and aggregation, designed to assess behaviors that extend beyond mere contextual searching. In our study, LServe-N represents the token budget allocated for dynamic sparsity, symbolized by N. Importantly, when dealing with long-context inputs, LServe’s latency isn’t solely determined by attention mechanisms; both the page selector and GEMM significantly contribute to it. Our experimental findings indicate that LServe-8192 experiences only a marginal slowdown, being up to 6% slower than LServe-4096 when sequence lengths surpass the 128K mark. In terms of accuracy across different sequence lengths (32K, 64K, 128K, 160K, 192K, 256K), we observe the following scores: Dense model yields 90.5, 86.8, 83.8, 79.3, 79.6, and 79.4 respectively, whereas LServe-4096 results in scores of 91.0, 85.6, 81.0, 79.0, 76.1, and 75.7. Meanwhile, LServe-8192 achieves evaluations of 91.8, 86.1, 81.7, 81.2, 79.7, and 79.1. During the prefilling phase, we rely heavily on time-to-first-token (TTFT) as a significant metric, while for the decoding phase, our focus shifts towards minimizing the latency involved in per-token generation.

During decoding, although the attention kernel maintains constant complexity due to a capped number of historical KV tokens, the complexity of the page selector still scales linearly with sequence length. As illustrated in Figure 14, for a sequence length of 128K and a 4K token budget for sparse attention, the page selector (0.24 ms) is already twice as slow as the sparse attention kernel (0.12 ms). With our reusable page selector, however, LServe significantly reduces page selection overhead by a factor of C, where C is the reuse interval. We further show that LServe is resilient to different reuse interval choices. Table 5 demonstrates no significant performance degradation until the reuse interval exceeds 8, so we set it to 4 by default in LServe.

In Figure 15, we apply static sparsity by converting 50% of attention heads to streaming heads, achieving a 1.3-1.7× speedup across various input sequence lengths. Additionally, we introduce dynamic sparsity with a fixed KV budget of 4096 tokens, which bounds the computational complexity of decoding attention to a constant, delivering a 30× speedup over the dense baseline for an input length of 256K. Although sparsity selection introduces minor overhead for shorter sequences, this is mitigated by reusable page selection. Additionally, we also perform the end-to-end ablation study in Section 5.5. 5.5 End-to-End Speedup Breakdown In Figure 16, we highlight the sources of performance improvement in LServe. By leveraging static sparsity, LServe achieves end-to-end speedups of up to 1.7× over the dense baseline. Additionally, dynamic sparsity, aided by a reusable page selector, significantly reduces generation latency, yielding a 7.7× speedup for sequence lengths of 256K. Lastly, LServe configures sparse patterns through offline profiling, effectively avoiding slowdowns from dynamic sparsity at shorter context lengths. 6 RELATED WORK LLM Serving Systems. Various systems have been developed to enhance LLM deployment efficiency. Orca (Yu et al., 2022) uses iteration-level scheduling and selective batching for distributed systems. vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b) introduces PagedAttention, inspired by virtual memory, to optimize KV cache management. TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) is the industry’s leading solution also featuring inflight batching and PagedAttention inspired by vLLM. LightLLM (Contributors, 2023a) further reduces memory waste in PagedAttention by introducing TokenAttention. SGLang (Zheng et al., 2023) advances LLM programming with a domain-specific language and RadixAttention. LMDeploy (Contributors, 2023b) improves deployment with persistent batching and blocked KV cache. Nanoflow (Zhu et al., 2024) features intra-device scheduling and asynchronous CPU scheduling, while QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) improves LLM serving throughput through W4A8KV4 quantization and system codesign. MLC-LLM (team, 2023) accelerates deployment on edge devices via compiler-based optimizations. Inspired by contextual sparsity (Liu et al., 2023), PowerInfer (Song et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2024b) deploys LLMs on memory-constrained devices via offloading.
contents.AI: Context Pooling Overhead. In order to facilitate the page selection process during the decoding stage, it is essential to compute representative features beforehand using min-max pooling during the prefilling phase. Notably, each pooling kernel accomplishes this task in less than 1 millisecond, while the entire prefilling process, when dealing with a context length of 128K, is completed in around 17 seconds. As a result, the overhead related to context pooling is negligible. Conversely, dynamic sparsity can realize up to a 4.5× complete speedup on longer sequences. The findings are derived from measurements with Llama3-8B using a unit batch size. 5.4 Sparse Attention Kernel for Decoding Stage Our examination focuses on analyzing different sparsity patterns in decoding attention. Figure 15 demonstrates the application of static sparsity, where 50% of the attention heads are converted into streaming heads, achieving a speedup of between 1.3 and 1.7 times across various input sequence lengths. Moreover, by applying dynamic sparsity with a set KV budget of 4096 tokens, we constrain the decoding attention’s computational complexity to a constant level. This delivers a 30× speedup compared to the dense baseline for input lengths of 256K. Although the selection of sparsity introduces minor overhead when dealing with shorter sequences, this is mitigated by leveraging reusable page selection. Additionally, the end-to-end ablation study is conducted in Section 5.5. 5.5 Comprehensive Breakdown of End-to-End Speedup In Figure 16, the sources contributing to performance enhancements in LServe are presented. By integrating static sparsity, LServe attains end-to-end speeds that are up to 1.7 times faster than the dense baseline. Enhancements through dynamic sparsity, supported by a reusable page selector, significantly minimize generation latency, achieving a remarkable 7.7× speedup for sequence lengths reaching 256K. Furthermore, LServe effectively configures sparse patterns through offline profiling, thereby avoiding delays associated with dynamic sparsity in shorter contexts. 6 RELATED WORK LLM Deployment Systems. Multiple innovative systems have been crafted to elevate the efficiency of large language model (LLM) deployment. Orca (Yu et al., 2022) employs iteration-level scheduling alongside selective batching tailored for distributed systems. vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b) introduces PagedAttention, which draws inspiration from virtual memory concepts to enhance KV cache management. Likewise, TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023), a much-celebrated industry solution, also includes inflight batching and PagedAttention as inspired by vLLM. Meanwhile, LightLLM (Contributors, 2023a) diminishes memory wastage in PagedAttention by incorporating TokenAttention. SGLang (Zheng et al., 2023) propels forward LLM programming through the adoption of a domain-specific language and RadixAttention mechanism. LMDeploy (Contributors, 2023b) ameliorates deployment through persistent batching and a blocked KV cache. In an analogous vein, Nanoflow (Zhu et al., 2024) boasts features such as intra-device scheduling and asynchronous CPU scheduling. QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) significantly boosts LLM serving throughput by employing W4A8KV4 quantization coupled with system co-design. MLC-LLM (team, 2023) delivers accelerated deployment on edge devices via compiler-based optimizations. Furthermore, drawing from ideas of contextual sparsity (Liu et al., 2023), PowerInfer (Song et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2024b) facilitates the deployment of LLMs on devices with limited memory by utilizing offloading strategies.

contents.human: Sparse Attention. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) reduces attention complexity by blending local, global, and random attention masks. Subsequent methods like StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024) simplify attention patterns by discarding KV caches mid-way through the context. However, these approaches struggle to retain the original models’ long-context capabilities due to limited global context modeling. Recent works like DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2024a), and SeerAttention (Gao et al., 2024) address this issue by introducing retrieval heads (Wu et al., 2024) or combining full attention with local attention heads. Quest (Tang et al., 2024) introduces dynamic, query-aware sparsity for accelerated decoding, while MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) extends similar ideas to the prefilling stage. FastGen (Ge et al., 2023) optimizes decoding by profiling attention heads to discard tokens. PQCache (Zhang et al., 2024a) and ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2024) further advance the selective attention methods with product quantization and low-rank decomposition. Additionally, LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023) finetunes shortcontext LLMs to long-context ones after converting global attention to shifted sparse attention. 7 CONCLUSION We introduce LServe, an efficient serving system for longsequence LLMs that leverages hybrid sparse attention. By incorporating unified block sparse attention, we achieve significant acceleration of the attention mechanism for both LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention 12 prefilling and decoding stages in long-sequence models. We further show that head-level static sparsity and query-aware dynamic sparsity are orthogonal and can be effectively combined with minimal impact on accuracy. LServe surpasses state-of-the-art systems, delivering an average of 1.3×-2.1× speedup in the decoding stage and up to 2.9× speedup in the prefilling stage, preserving the models’ long-context capabilities. contents.AI: Sparse Attention is a concept in attention mechanisms, exemplified by BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020), which manages to lower attention computational complexity by using a mixture of local, global, and random attention patterns. Following this, methods such as StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024) aim to simplify attention models further by removing KV caches partway through the context processing. Nevertheless, these strategies often fall short in retaining the original models’ capabilities for handling long-contexts effectively, primarily due to their restricted modeling of global context. More recent innovations like DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2024a), and SeerAttention (Gao et al., 2024) work to overcome this limitation by incorporating retrieval heads, as discussed by Wu et al., 2024 or by fusing full attention with local attention heads. In another approach, Quest (Tang et al., 2024) proposes dynamic, query-driven sparsity to hasten decoding, while MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) applies related concepts at the prefilling stage. Furthermore, FastGen (Ge et al., 2023) enhances the decoding phase by evaluating and eliminating tokens based on attention heads. Innovations like PQCache (Zhang et al., 2024a) and ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2024) make strides in selective attention methods by employing product quantization and low-rank decomposition techniques, respectively. Meanwhile, LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023) adapts shorter-context LLMs into longer-context models by transforming global attention into a modified sparse attention strategy. In 7 CONCLUSION, we unveil LServe, a groundbreaking system optimized for serving lengthy LLM sequences efficiently by utilizing a hybrid sparse attention approach. By incorporating a unified block sparse attention, LServe significantly enhances the speed of attention mechanisms during both the prefilling and decoding phases in models handling long sequences. Moreover, our findings reveal that integrating head-level static sparsity with query-aware dynamic sparsity is feasible and effective, maintaining minimal impact on accuracy. LServe not only excels over current leading systems but also delivers an impressive average speedup of 1.3×-2.1× during the decoding stage and up to a 2.9× speedup during the prefilling stage, all while preserving long-context processing capabilities. name of paper: Does Ideological Polarization Lead to Policy Polarization?
summary: I analyze an election involving two parties who are both officeand policy-motivated and who are ideologically polarized. One party may possess a valence advantage. The parties compete by proposing policies on a second policy issue. The analysis reveals a subtle relationship between ideological polarization and policy polarization. If ideologies are highly dispersed, there is a U-shaped relationship between ideological polarization and platform polarization. In contrast, if ideological dispersion is limited, increasing ideological polarization generally results in policy moderation. In both cases, valence plays no role in policy polarization. Finally, as in Buisseret and van Weelden (2022), adding ideological polarization adds nuance on the effects of increasing valence: both highand low-valence candidates may adopt more extreme positions, depending on the electorate’s degree of ideological polarization.

Moreover, it considers the possibility that one of these parties could hold an edge in terms of valence.

contents.AI: The political parties engage in competition by presenting policies concerning an additional issue. The study uncovers a complex interplay between ideological polarization and policy polarization. When there is a wide spread of ideologies, a U-shaped correlation emerges between ideological polarization and the polarization of platforms. Conversely, when ideological dispersion is narrow, an escalation in ideological polarization often brings about policy moderation. In both scenarios, valence is irrelevant to policy polarization. Moreover, akin to findings by Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), introducing ideological polarization complicates the understanding of increasing valence effects: candidates with either high or low valence might adopt more extreme stances, contingent on the level of ideological polarization within the electorate. For correspondence: pdenter@eco.uc3m.es. 1 arXiv:2502.14712v1 [econ.TH] 20 Feb 2025 1 Introduction In multiple democratic societies globally, polarization has escalated significantly over recent years. For instance, Abramowitz and Saunders (2008) highlight that “ideological polarization has increased dramatically among the mass public in the United States as well as among political elites.“ Boxell, Gentzkow, and Shapiro (2024) observe a rising trend of polarization since the 1980s in countries like the US, Canada, Switzerland, France, and New Zealand, while Carothers and O’Donohue (2019) report a similar rise in polarization in nations such as Kenya, Indonesia, Turkey, and Poland. It is widely presumed that this increasing polarization is harmful to the effective operation of democratic decision-making, as it can hinder learning and impede compromise between parties. However, the impact of escalating polarization among different social factions on policy-making remains ambiguous. Should we anticipate a correlation where greater polarization in society leads to a heightened polarization of policies? Or is an alternate scenario likely? Empirical evidence does not present a straightforward conclusion. Figure 1 illustrates changes in both affective polarization (left panel) and policy polarization (right panel) in the US since 1998.1 The visualization Figure 1: displays the divergence in ideologies (left) and policy platforms in the US from 1998 onwards and demonstrates that affective polarization has steadily increased. Initially, policy polarization decreased before experiencing an upturn around the year 2008. In this paper, I aim to offer a game-theoretical exploration of how shifts in affective polarization influence policy polarization. Politically motivated parties, driven by both office and policy objectives and polarized along an ideological dimension that does not pertain to policy, determine which policy proposals to present to the electorate in their pursuit of election. 1Affective polarization is quantified as the difference in average DW nominate scores in both the House and Senate for Republicans and Democrats, whereas policy polarization is measured as the difference in the rile variable of Republicans and Democrats according to the Manifesto Project Database (Lehmann, Franzmann, Al-Gaddooa, Burst, Ivanusch, Regel, Riethmüller, Volkens, Weßels, and Zehnter, 2024). 2

contents.human: I show that increasing ideological polarization always decreases platform polarization if ideological polarization is low. When ideological polarization is large, then the effect of increasing it depends on how dispersed ideologies are: if ideological dispersion is low, then further increasing ideological polarization at some point will lead to perfect convergence in policies at the center of the policy space. However, in a society with highly dispersed ideologies, increasing polarization further leads to increasing policy polarization as well. Hence, the relationship between affective polarization and policy polarization is U-shaped as in Figure 1. The paper also shows that changing valence levels has no effect on policy polarization in any interior equilibrium. However, valence levels, together with affective polarization, determine which party adopts a more extreme and which a more centrist position. Therefore, just as in Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), adding polarization as a determinant of policy choices adds significant nuance to the model’s predictions, and valence and policy congruence could be both positively and negatively correlated. Literature: The paper contributes to a wide array of literature in political economy. First and foremost, it contributes to the literature studying the determinants of polarization of policies. Alesina and Rosenthal (2000) show that if policies are determined by a executivelegislative compromise, voter behavior tends to moderate policies, which in turn creates incentives to choose more radical policy platforms. Polborn and Snyder (2017) show that polarization may increase in legislative competition if elections outcomes become more uncertain. Prummer (2020) shows that a more fragmented media landscape leads to an increase in polarization when parties can micro-target voters during a campaign. Similarly, Balart, Casas, and Troumpounis (2022) study how modern information technology, that allows for more precise targeting of voters during an electoral campaign, may induce policy polarization. Yuksel (2022) shows that in fractionalized societies polarization of policies tends to be greater when voters need to spend time to learn about policy parties’ multi-dimensional platforms. Matakos, Troumpounis, and Xefteris (2015, 2016) study how different degrees of rule-disproportionality of electoral systems affect policies. Levy and Razin (2015) show that greater polarization of opinions caused by correlation neglect may lead to less polarization of policies. Denter (2021) shows that greater valence leads to policy moderation if there are complementarities between policy and valence. In contrast to all of these paper, the focus in the current paper is how ideological polarization impacts policies. The paper also contributes to the literature studying the implications of differences in valence, pioneered by Stokes (1963). Ansolabehere and Snyder (2000), Groseclose (2001), 3 and Aragones and Palfrey (2002) study models of electoral competition and policy motivated candidates and show that candidates with a valence advantage tend to choose more moderate positions that their disadvantages counterparts. A very closely related paper is Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022). They enrich the model of electoral competition between office motivated candidates by introducing fixed candidate ideology as a third characteristic. Their analysis reveals that if the weight of ideology in voters utility function is high enough, i.e., if societies are polarized, then the standard result in the literature that the candidate with the valence advantage takes the more moderate position may change. That is similar to the analysis in Xefteris (2014), who extends the classical model to three candidates and shows that when there is significant uncertainty about voters’ preferences, then the candidate with the greatest valence may choose the most extreme policy position. Aragones and Xefteris (2017), consider a model in which voters may be heterogeneous in how they evaluate candidates’ non-policy characteristics. They demonstrate that policy polarization follows a U-shaped pattern concerning the proportion of voters supporting the more popular candidate. The current paper is closely related to Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), but allows for policy motivation on the candidates’ side and uncertainty about the election outcome draws not from uncertainty about voters bliss points but from aggregate shows to the share of voters supporting a given candidate. The analysis reveals that valence has no impact whatsoever on policy polarization, but it determines which candidates locates closer to the political center. If societies are sufficiently polarized, then the candidate or party with the valence advantage may take a less extreme position. Finally, the paper contributes to the literature studying electoral competition when positions on a subset of policy issues are fixed. The pioneering article in this field is due to Krasa and Polborn (2010), in which they study a model of electoral competition with office-motivated candidates. There are multiple binary policy issues, and candidates are exogenously committed to fixed positions on some issues while choosing positions on the remaining ones. Buisseret and Van Weelden (2020) consider a variant of their model with two issues and two incumbent politicians, who hold fixed and opposing positions on one of these dimensions and can freely choose policies in the other. The novelty in their model is that they allow for an outsider candidate to challenge the incumbents. They show that the incumbents are particularly vulnerable to the entry of the outsider when ideological polarization is high. Hughes (2024) also considers a variant of Krasa and Polborn (2010) to study strategic voting in legislative elections. He shows that in legislative elections equilibrium policies are both more predictable and more representative of voter preferences than in sin4 gle district elections. The current paper differs in that, while parties occupy fixed ideological positions, they are free to choose policy in a second, continuous policy dimension. The focus is thereby to highlight how ideological polarization impacts the polarization of policies.
contents.AI: I demonstrate that an increase in ideological polarization invariably leads to decreased platform polarization when the initial level of ideological polarization is low. On the other hand, when ideological polarization is already substantial, the impact of increasing it hinges on the extent of ideological dispersion. If the dispersion is minimal, then further amplifying ideological polarization eventually results in a perfect convergence of policies to the center of the policy spectrum. Conversely, in contexts where ideologies are widely dispersed, additional polarization tends to intensify policy polarization. As a result, the connection between affective polarization and policy polarization assumes a U-shaped trajectory, as illustrated in Figure 1. Additionally, the research indicates that alterations in valence levels do not affect policy polarization in any scenario of internal equilibrium. However, it is noted that valence levels together with affective polarization shape which political party adopts a more extreme versus a more centrist stance. Consequently, similar to the findings of Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), incorporating polarization as a determinant of policy decisions adds significant complexity to the model’s predictions, and consequently, valence and policy congruence can be both positively and negatively associated.Literature: This research contributes significantly to a broad spectrum of political economy literature. Primarily, it enriches the discussion surrounding the determinants of policy polarization. Alesina and Rosenthal (2000) have shown that when policies emerge from executive-legislative compromises, voter behavior often moderates policies, creating incentives for the selection of more radical policy platforms. Similarly, Polborn and Snyder (2017) highlight that increased polarization may occur in legislative competition if election outcomes become unpredictable. Furthermore, Prummer (2020) argues that a more fragmented media landscape exacerbates polarization when political parties can micro-target voters during campaigns. Analogous to this, Balart, Casas, and Troumpounis (2022) examine how contemporary information technology, which enables precision targeting of voters in electoral campaigns, could foster policy polarization. Yuksel (2022) asserts that in fragmented societies, the policy polarization is exacerbated when voters must invest time to comprehend political parties’ multidimensional platforms. Matakos, Troumpounis, and Xefteris (2015, 2016) explore how varying degrees of electoral system disproportionality impact policies. Levy and Razin (2015) demonstrate that increased opinion polarization due to correlation neglect can result in diminished policy polarization. Denter (2021) argues that higher valence leads to policy moderation in scenarios where there are complementaries between policy and valence. Distinctly, the current paper focuses on the influence of ideological polarization on policy outcomes. It also adds to the literature examining the effects of valence differences, a line of inquiry initiated by Stokes (1963). Ansolabehere and Snyder (2000), Groseclose (2001), and Aragones and Palfrey (2002) explore electoral competition models with policy-driven candidates, illustrating that candidates with a valence edge tend to pursue more moderate positions compared to their less advantaged counterparts.A closely related study by Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022) enriches the electoral competition model between candidates driven by office ambitions by incorporating fixed candidate ideology as a critical factor. Their findings indicate that, in highly polarized societies, the conventional outcome where a candidate with a valence advantage assumes a more moderate position might not hold. This analysis mirrors insights from Xefteris (2014), who adapts the classical electoral model to include three candidates, revealing that substantial uncertainty about voter preferences may lead a candidate with high valence to select an extreme policy stance. Aragones and Xefteris (2017) present a model where voters vary in their evaluation of candidates’ non-policy attributes. They show that policy polarization exhibits a U-shaped pattern relative to the proportion of voters backing the more popular candidate. While this paper shares foundational aspects with Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), it uniquely allows for candidate policy motivation, with uncertainty emanating not from voter preference bliss points but from shifts in the aggregate voter support for a candidate. This analysis illustrates that valence exerts no influence on policy polarization directly but does determine which candidate aligns closer to the political center. If societal polarization is high enough, the candidate or party with a valence advantage might opt for a less extreme policy position. Lastly, this research also contributes to the examination of electoral competition when party positions on certain policy issues remain fixed. Krasa and Polborn (2010) pioneered this field by investigating a model focusing on electoral competition with office-seeking candidates. In their scenario, there are multiple binary issues where candidates are committed to specific positions while selecting policies on others. Buisseret and Van Weelden (2020) extend this model by introducing an outsider challenge against incumbents holding fixed, divergent positions on one dimension but having policy latitude on others. In their model’s innovation, they allow for an outsider candidate who can disrupt incumbent positions, particularly when ideological polarization is pronounced. Hughes (2024) explores a similar model, analyzing strategic voting in legislative elections, concluding that equilibrium outcomes in such elections are more stable and accurately reflect voter preferences than in single-district races. Distinctly, this paper allows for parties to hold fixed ideological stances while flexibly choosing policy positions along a continuous second dimension, focusing on how ideological polarization influences policy polarization outcomes.

contents.human: The paper proceeds as follows. In Section 2 I introduce the model and define an equilibrium. In Section 3, I solve the model and derive the paper’s main results. Section 4 concludes. All formal proofs are relegated to the appendix.
contents.AI: The structure of this paper unfolds in the following manner. I begin with Section 2, where I present the model and offer a definition of equilibrium. Moving on to Section 3, I address the solution of the model and extract the primary results of the paper. The final remarks are covered in Section 4. Any formal proofs can be found in the appendix for further exploration.

contents.human: 2 Model Two parties, i ∈{L, R}, compete in an election. There are two policy dimensions d ∈{1, 2}. Dimension 1 represents party ideology. I assume that parties are polarized on this dimension, representing the traditional issue cleavage between parties, for example, the conflict between a conservative and a liberal party. In particular, party L occupies p1 L = 0, while party R has p1 R = 1. Dimension 2 represents a policy issue such as tax or trade policy.
