LServe integrates various sparsity patterns into a unified framework. sparse attention patterns are unified within a block-sparse formulation (Figure 4), and are flexibly supported through fused CUDA kernels. LServe also supports weight, activation and KV quantization, which significantly improves generation throughput at shorter context lengths. 3.1 Unified Block Sparse Attention As shown in Figure 3, skipping computations in the attention kernel by blockwise processing accelerates execution by shortening the sequential loop. Building on this, we introduce a unified block sparse attention pattern for both the prefilling and decoding stages: each thread block computes a TQ × TK tile (and TK × TV ) in parallel. Here, TQ > 1 in the prefilling stage and TQ = 1 in the decoding stage, with TK (or TV ) corresponding to the page size in PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023a). We define block sparsity in LServe as follows: for each TQ × TK tile in the attention calculation, it is either fully skipped (Figure 4(b), light gray blocks) or retained as in standard causal attention (Figure 4(b), blue blocks). Given that each GPU streaming multiprocessor can execute only a limited number of thread blocks simultaneously, the attention kernel execution time can be approximated by the total count of TQ × TK (and TK × TV ) blocks. With a block sparsity of r, where rN of the N total blocks are empty, the theoretical speedup from block sparse attention is 1/(1 -r). For example in Figure 4(b), 10 out of N=21 blocks are non-empty. Thus, the theoretical speedup ratio is 2.1×. Figure 4(c)(d) shows two sparsity patterns used in LServe. The first is streaming attention (Figure 4(c)), a specialized form of block-sparse attention where each token only attends to its immediate neighbors and initial tokens, known as attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2023). Unlike dense attention, where computation for each row scales with the token index, streaming attention keeps the computation for each token constant-in this case, only two local blocks and one sink block, as shown in Figure 4(c). This pattern is nearly costfree in applications with extremely long contexts. Because streaming attention follows a fixed pattern, we designate which heads use it in offline, and make it static for different input sequences in both prefilling and decoding. The second type of sparsity, illustrated in Figure 4(d), is page sparsity, which is specifically designed for the decoding stage where TQ = 1 applies to both skipped and selected pages. Unlike streaming attention, page sparsity in LServe is dynamic, allowing different query tokens to attend to different KV pages. As noted in Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023), dynamic sparsity results in higher compression ratios than static sparsity. Our observations indicate that static sparsity offers up to a 2× efficiency gain, whereas dynamic sparsity bounds the decoding complexity to a constant, with each query attending only to a fixed number of KV tokens. 3.2 LServe System Overview We present an overview of LServe in Figure 5. Built on QServe, which natively supports quantized LLMs, LServe enhances the baseline system by introducing sparsity into both prefilling and decoding dataflows. The two-way paged KV cache serves as the bridge between these two stages. As discussed in Section 3.1, we statically partition the attention heads of a pretrained LLM into two groups: dense heads and streaming heads. Unlike conventional LLM serving systems, which maintain a single KV cache, we utilize separate KV caches for the dense and streaming heads. The KV cache for the streaming heads is organized similarly to the pages in QServe, with scaling factors and zero points stored immediately after the token features. Additionally, the KV cache for the dense heads includes key statistics that facilitate critical page selection during the decoding stage. In the prefilling stage, the key differences between LServe and conventional dense-attention LLM serving systems are twofold: (1) we replace the dense attention kernel with our unified block sparse attention kernel, and (2) we write back quantized KV features using two distinct kernels. In the decoding stage, our system incorporates dynamic attention sparsity. Rather than developing an entirely new dynamic sparse attention kernel, we decompose the problem into two components: (1) dynamic page selection and (2) a dense attention kernel with shorter page tables, where the shorter page tables are provided by the page selector. Notably, our page selector employs hierarchical paging and reusable page selection, enhancing both long-context accuracy and page selection efficiency. contents.AI: In LLM (Large Language Model) serving, one of the main challenges is the highly variable and unpredictable generation length of each sequence. Simply padding all sequences to the maximum length leads to significant memory wastage and fragmentation. To tackle this problem, vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b) introduces an inventive KV cache management algorithm, PagedAttention, which draws inspiration from the virtual memory systems used in operating systems. Instead of dedicating a continuous memory buffer to each sequence’s KV cache, PagedAttention cleverly splits the cache into fixed-size blocks or pages. Each of these pages holds KV data for a specific number of consecutive tokens, usually ranging between 16 to 64. This design choice is facilitated by a page block table that logs the physical address of each page, enabling the PagedAttention kernel to retrieve KV features using indirect addressing. Implementations like TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) and QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) have embraced quantized page attention, which effectively diminishes memory bandwidth usage during decoding, resulting in superior generation speed.The issue of serving long-sequence language models is primarily challenging due to the high computational demands of attention mechanisms. As depicted in Figure 2, for Llama-3-8B with a batch size of 1 and varying sequence lengths using the A100 GPU, attention kernels constitute a substantial portion of runtime-50% at sequences over 64k and up to 75% at 128k. According to QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), this proportion of attention kernel time relative to total runtime increases with batch size, underscoring the importance of optimizing attention for effective real-world deployment. Enhancing attention in long-sequence LLMs requires a thorough comprehension of attention kernel implementation on GPUs, showcased in Figure 3. In the prefilling stage, query tokens iterate sequentially over all key and value tokens in a block-by-block fashion. The number of sequential iterations can be reduced by skipping KV blocks, thereby accelerating attention. Parallelization occurs across batch size, attention heads, and query tokens during prefilling, with sequences having one query token in decoding, whereas calculations along the KV token dimension remain sequential. Each block, represented as a grid with an orange contour in Figure 3, is computed collaboratively by threads within a thread block. While skipping computations within blocks could be considered, it typically provides limited speedups, as faster threads must wait for slower ones due to lockstep execution within a GPU warp. Thus, a more effective acceleration strategy involves reducing the sequential iterations along the KV token dimension, leading to a unified block sparse attention formulation. In this setup, the attention computation is skipped in a blockwise manner, where unnecessary blocks are either fully processed or completely ignored during prefilling. During decoding, sequences consist of a single query token, reducing the dimensionality of each block to 1×P, where P reflects the page size or count of KV tokens per page. We’ll elaborate on LServe’s sparsity pattern selection in Section 3. Additionally, as the decoding stage is memory-bound, KV cache quantization contributes to improved performance. This quantization operates orthogonally to block sparsity: quantization decreases runtime per iteration, while sparsity decreases the number of iterations.Introducing LServe: a novel system for efficient LLM serving with sparse attention over long sequences. LServe incorporates various sparse attention patterns into a singular framework, as shown in Figure 4, thereby enabling flexible support via unified CUDA kernels. The system also accommodates weight, activation, and KV quantization, markedly enhancing generation throughput, especially at reduced context lengths. The system uses a unified block sparse attention approach, as depicted in Figure 3. By skipping computations through blockwise processing, this method accelerates execution by shortening sequential loops. We establish a unified block sparse attention pattern applicable to both prefilling and decoding stages, whereby each thread block computes a TQ × TK tile and TK × TV in parallel. TQ exceeds 1 during prefilling, but is 1 during decoding-where TK, or TV, represents the page size in PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023a). Block sparsity in LServe means each TQ × TK calculation tile is entirely processed or skipped. Each GPU streaming multiprocessor can execute multiple thread blocks concurrently, and attention kernel execution time hinges on the count of TQ × TK, or TK × TV blocks. Given a block sparsity ratio r, with rN of N blocks empty, the anticipated speedup resulting from block sparse attention equates to 1/(1 -r). For instance, in Figure 4(b), 10 out of N=21 blocks are non-empty, indicating a theoretical 2.1× speedup. Figure 4(c)(d) reveals two LServe sparsity patterns. The first, streaming attention (Figure 4(c)), restricts each token’s attention to immediate neighbors and initial tokens, maintaining constant computational needs per token-two local blocks and one sink block, as in Figure 4(c). This is notably cost-efficient for applications with extensive contexts. Given its fixed nature, we offline designate which heads employ this streaming attention for various input sequences in prefilling and decoding. Alternatively, Figure 4(d) highlights page sparsity intended for decoding stages where TQ is 1 for all pages-both skipped and accessed. In contrast to streaming attention, LServe’s dynamic page sparsity allows different query tokens to focus on distinct KV pages. Dynamic sparsity offers higher compression ratios than static sparsity, as noted in Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023). Static sparsity often yields up to a 2× efficiency improvement, whereas dynamic sparsity confines decoding complexity to a constant due to fixed KV token attendance per query.Offering an overview of LServe as shown in Figure 5, this system builds upon QServe, inherently supporting quantized language models. LServe enhances its baseline by integrating sparsity into prefilling and decoding dataflows. A dual-page KV cache bridges these operations. Per Section 3.1, attention heads of a pretrained LLM are partitioned into dense and streaming groups, diverging from typical single KV cache practice. Streaming heads mirror QServe pages for KV cache organization, immediately following token features with zero points and scaling factors. Dense heads’ KV cache integrates key statistics for optimal page selection in decoding. In prefilling, LServe diverges from traditional dense-attention LLM systems by substituting unified block sparse attention kernels and writing quantized KV features through separate kernels. Decoding employs dynamic attention sparsity, not via a novel dynamic sparse attention kernel but through (1) dynamic page selection, and (2) dense attention kernel application with reduced page tables-the page selector supplies these shorter tables. Our page selector utilizes hierarchical paging and reusable selection, elevating both contextual accuracy and page selection efficiency in the system.

We omit normalization layers and residual connections in this figure for the sake of simplicity. 3.3 Prefilling Stage: Sparsity Determination We adopt the approach from DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024) to classify each attention head as either a retrieval head or a streaming head. Using DuoAttention’s optimization-based identification method, we obtain a gating value α ∈[0, 1] for each head, where values closer to 1 signify a retrieval head, and values closer to 0 indicate a streaming head. To classify a head as a retrieval head, we compare α to a threshold τ, determined by a sparsity quantile. For instance, with a target sparsity of 50% across attention heads, τ equals the median of all gate values, thereby designating half of the heads as retrieval heads. 3.4 Prefilling Stage: Kernel Implementation To effectively translate sparsity into performance gains, it is essential to avoid iterating over a complete sequential loop and relying on conditional statements to determine data loading and computation requirements. This method is inefficient for GPU computation patterns, which thrive on minimizing branching within loops. Instead, we should focus on iterating only over the necessary blocks by accurately calculating offsets to load data and assess whether a block should be processed. To facilitate this, we introduce an iterator-based abstraction that standardizes indexing operations. This allows us to loop exclusively over the blocks requiring computation, with data offsets easily computed using offset = iter(i + 1) -iter(i). This abstraction efficiently skips unnecessary blocks with minimal overhead and necessitates few changes to the kernel function, thus enhancing maintainability. Take the streaming heads as an example, the iterators are determined outside the attention kernel since streaming heads are configured offline and the attention pattern is fixed. Once the attention on sink tokens is complete, the iterator automatically updates the memory pointer to the first local token in the KV cache with minimal overhead. Additionally, our iterator-based formulation unifies the more general block sparse pattern (see Figure 4). 3.5 Decoding Stage: Sparsity Determination To further enhance the long-context LLM decoding throughput, we introduce dynamic sparsity upon the input-agnostic static sparsity in Sec. 3.1. 3.5.1 Challenge: the Page Size Dilemma In the decoding stage, the attention operation is memorybound, so state-of-the-art systems typically implement KV cache quantization to reduce device memory usage and enhance throughput. However, this quantization introduces challenges for further optimization. Specifically, reducing the bit-width of KV tokens necessitates larger page sizes to maintain GPU memory bandwidth utilization. Failure to do so can lead to significant throughput loss (Table 1). Yet, LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention 6 Accuracy 0.0 0.2 0.8 1.0 Accuracy 0.0 0.2 0.8 1.0 Accuracy 0.0 0.2 0.8 1.0 43K 85K 128K 171K 211K 256K 0K 0 22 44 67 89 43K 85K 128K 171K 211K 256K 0K (b) Page Size: 16, Token Budget: 4096 0 22 44 67 89 0 22 44 67 89 43K 85K 128K 171K 211K 256K 0K 43K 85K 128K 171K 211K 256K 0K (e) Page Size: 32, Token Budget: 8192 43K 85K 128K 171K 211K 256K 0K 0 22 44 67 89 43K 85K 128K 171K 211K 256K 0K 0 22 44 67 89 (f) Page Size: 64, Token Budget: 16384 Document Depth (%) 0 22 44 67 89 43K 85K 128K 171K 211K 256K 0K (a) Dense Attention (c) Page Size: 32, Token Budget: 4096 (d) Page Size: 64, Token Budget: 4096 Document Depth (%) Document Depth (%) Document Length Document Length Figure 6: We evaluate the Llama-3-8B model with the Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) (Kamradt, 2024) benchmarks. This observation poses challenges to balance between accuracy and efficiency. 3.5.2 Hierarchical Paging: Mitigating the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff We observe that the failure of query-aware KV cache selection paradigm (Figure 6) is not due to the coarser granularity of sparse attention (i.e., larger page size). Rather, the underlying cause lies in that page-wise statistical indicators become homogenized and less representative especially when there are excessive tokens within a single page. To address this issue, we design a simple-yet-effective hierarchical paging system that introduces an abstract layer of virtual logical page for estimating token criticality, while preserving the original memory layout of KV cache in (physical pages). As illustrated in Figure 7, our hierarchical paging groups NL tokens into a logical page and NP tokens into a physical page (NP = g · NL, g ∈Z), that is, a physical page contains g logical pages. If these important tokens are randomly and sparsely distributed in the context, chances are that all logical pages in P are scattered in different physical pages, that is, for any P1, P2 ∈P, i1 ̸= i2. In this case, all |P| physical pages (|P| · NP tokens) are selected to avoid losing important information. Consequently, our hierarchical paging may suffer from a decrease in attention sparsity by NP /NL. Fortunately, the semantic continuity of natural language endows the attention operation with intrinsic locality, allowing LServe to maintain a consistent sparse attention token budget for larger physical page sizes. During the decoding stage, the coherence of contextual tokens makes the current query token incline to attend to consecutive pages in the KV cache. As a result, logical pages with highest importance scores tend to cluster within similar physical pages. This kind of spatial locality effectively alleviates the need for a increased token budget, thereby reducing the overhead caused by the contradiction between quantization and sparse attention. Experimental results in Figure 13 further affirm that our hierarchical paging well preserves the model accuracy even with the same token budget as the vanilla page selector with smaller page sizes. Moreover, the attention mechanism in decoding stage also exhibits the temporal locality: adjacent query tokens also heavily attend to similar historical pages. And there is no need for queries at consecutive decoding steps to select salient pages independently. Instead, the page selection decision can be shared across queries, aligning with the block-sparse attention formulation illustrated in Figure 4(d). When the number of history tokens surpasses 64K, the na ̈ıve page selector becomes the bottleneck to system efficiency, whereas our reusable page selector significantly alleviates this problem. 3.6 Decoding Stage: Kernel Implementation During the decoding stage, attention heads are processed in parallel on GPU, enabling different sparsity patterns to be applied independently on each head. This flexibility enables some heads to operate with page-level sparsity while others follow the streaming computation pattern. To leverage this, we employ a two-level indexing hierarchy to unify the operations for streaming heads and dense heads with dynamic sparsity. Specifically, the low-level (physical) index corresponds to the iteration step of current GPU thread, which executes in a consecutive manner as in dense attention, while logical index denotes the actual position of the target token within the entire KV cache. For each dense head, the page selector provides an index table to map physical index to logical index. Streaming heads are treated as dynamic sparse heads with index table only containing the sink and local pages. During the initial prefilling stage, LServe handles both dense and streaming heads using a hybrid sparse attention kernel. The previously stored Keys and Values are divided into two separate paging systems to cater to streaming and dense heads, respectively. As the system transitions to the decoding stage, LServe utilizes dynamic sparsity specifically on the dense heads, selecting only certain KV Pages for decoding process attention. For simplicity, normalization layers and residual connections are not shown in this diagram.3.3 Prefilling Stage: Sparsity DeterminationIn this stage, leveraging the DuoAttention method (Xiao et al., 2024), each attention head is classified as either a retrieval or streaming head. By employing DuoAttention’s optimization-based approach, a gating value α ∈[0, 1] is allocated for each head. Values nearing 1 suggest a retrieval head, while values approaching 0 denote a streaming head. A head is designated as a retrieval head when α surpasses a threshold τ, which is set by a sparsity quantile. For example, if the aim is a 50% sparsity rate among attention heads, τ is the median of all gate values, thus classifying half of the heads as retrieval.3.4 Prefilling Stage: Kernel ImplementationTo make sparsity enhance performance, it is critical to avoid iterating through an entire sequence loop and using conditional statements to determine how data is loaded and computations are made. Such methods are suboptimal for GPU operations, as these prefer minimizing branching within loops. Instead, we concentrate on iterating solely through necessary blocks by correctly calculating offsets for data loading and block processing decisions. To achieve this, we introduce an iterator-based abstraction that standardizes indexing operations. This innovation ensures that we loop only over blocks that need computation, with data offsets determined through offset = iter(i + 1) - iter(i). This method effectively skips unneeded blocks with minimal extra processing and requires only a few kernel function modifications, thus improving maintainability. For example, in streaming heads, iterators are determined outside the attention kernel since streaming heads are preset offline and maintain a fixed attention pattern. Once attention regarding sink tokens is finalized, the iterator seamlessly shifts the memory pointer to the initial local token in the KV cache with minimal processing requirement. Moreover, our iterator-based setup aligns with a more general block sparse pattern, as demonstrated in Figure 4.3.5 Decoding Stage: Sparsity DeterminationTo further enhance the decoding throughput of long-context LLMs, we overlay dynamic sparsity onto the static, input-agnostic sparsity described in Section 3.1.3.5.1 Challenge: the Page Size DilemmaDuring decoding, attention operations primarily consume memory, prompting leading systems to use KV cache quantization, which reduces memory usage and boosts throughput. However, quantization complicates optimization by necessitating larger page sizes to maintain GPU memory bandwidth usage effectively, lest significant throughput is lost (refer to Table 1). Larger KV page sizes make sparsification processes cumbersome; tools like Quest (Tang et al., 2024), which estimates token criticality using page-wise stats, fail as page size grows (illustrated in Figure 6). Balancing accuracy and efficiency thus becomes challenging.3.5.2 Hierarchical Paging: Mitigating the accuracy-efficiency tradeoffThe failure of query-aware KV cache selection, highlighted in Figure 6, originates not from larger sparse attention granularity (i.e., bigger page size) but because page-wise statistical indicators become too homogenized and less effective, especially with too many tokens on a single page. To combat this, we design a hierarchical paging system introducing an extra layer of virtual logical pages for token criticality estimation while preserving the original physical KV cache memory layout. In Figure 7, NL tokens are grouped into a logical page and NP tokens into a physical page (NP = g · NL, where g ∈Z), meaning each physical page contains g logical pages. Tokens within the same logical page contribute collectively to the same criticality assessment. In LServe, the channel-wise minimum and maximum values of keys within a logical page serve as its representative vectors, a metric proven effective (Tang et al., 2024) for estimating page importance particularly with moderate page sizes (≤16). The current query attends to each logical page’s representative vectors to compute the importance score as:$$ S_j = ∑D ( max(q[i] ·k_j^max[i]), q[i] ·k_j^min[i] ) $$Here, S is the importance score of the logical page, j ∈{a, b, ...} is the logical page index, i indexes the channel, and D is the head dimension. The importance of each physical page is determined by the maximum reduction over its corresponding logical pages’ importance scores. Finally, LServe selects the top-K physical pages (based on the predefined token budget) with the highest importance scores for input into the sparse attention kernel.3.5.3 Reducing sparse attention overheads with localityA pertinent question is: as the size of a physical page grows, will hierarchical paging demand a higher token budget to sustain accuracy in sparse attention? Suppose during a generation step, the most crucial historical tokens cluster in a logical page set P = {P(i, j)}, where i ∈{1, 2, ...}, j ∈{a, b, ...} denote the physical and logical indices of a page, respectively. If these key tokens are spread randomly and sparsely throughout the context, then it is likely all logical pages in P would be situated in separate physical pages, hence for any P1, P2 ∈ P, i1 ≠ i2. Consequently, all |P| physical pages (|P| · NP tokens) must be selected to avoid omitting essential information. Nevertheless, naive paging needs to only preserve |P| · NL tokens owing to its direct reduction of page sizes to a smaller scale (e.g., NL). Thus, our hierarchical paging can experience a decrease in attention sparsity by NP/NL. Thankfully, due to the natural proclivity of language, attention operations are inherently localized, thus enabling LServe to maintain a consistent sparse attention token budget even with larger physical page sizes. When decoding, the coherence of contextual tokens creates a tendency for the current query token to engage with successive pages in the KV cache. Consequently, logical pages with the highest importance scores are likely to be clustered within similar physical pages. This inherent spatial locality effectively reduces the need for a larger token budget, lessening overhead from the conflict between quantization and sparse attention. Experimental outcomes depicted in Figure 13 specify that our hierarchical paging preserves model accuracy well, even employing similar token budgets to those of smaller page size selectors. Moreover, the attention mechanism in the decoding phase also exhibits temporal locality: adjacent query tokens frequently attend to comparable historical pages, eliminating the need for queries at successive decoding stages to independently select important pages. Instead, the decision regarding page selection can be uniformly applied across queries, correlating with the block-sparse attention format shown in Figure 4(d). contents.human: Testbed. Our primary experiments are conducted on a server equipped with 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, 2 AMD EPYC 7763 CPUs (128 cores), and 2TB of memory. Unless explicitly stated, all experiments utilize the A100 GPUs. Additionally, we perform some evaluations on a cloud instance with a single NVIDIA L40S 48GB GPU to assess system performance across different GPU architectures. All evaluations use PyTorch 2.5.0 with CUDA 12.4 and cuDNN 9.2.0.
contents.AI: Testbed. In our primary series of experiments, we make use of a server that is outfitted with 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each boasting 80GB, along with 2 AMD EPYC 7763 CPUs that together provide 128 cores, and a substantial 2TB of memory. Unless we indicate otherwise, all our experimental procedures utilize the A100 GPUs. For further assessment, we also conduct evaluations on a cloud-based instance employing a single NVIDIA L40S 48GB GPU to examine the system’s performance across various GPU architectures. Every evaluation is executed using PyTorch version 2.5.0, accompanied by CUDA 12.4 and cuDNN 9.2.0.

contents.human: Models. To comprehensively assess system performance across various LLM architectures, we utilize the widely adopted GQA-based model Llama-3-8B (Dubey et al., 2024), the MHA-based model Llama-2-7B (Touvron et al., 2023), and the smaller-scale model Minitron-4B (Muralidharan et al., 2024). Additionally, to support long-context inference, we employ the context-extended Llama-3-8B version Gradient (Pekelis et al., 2024).
contents.AI: Models. In order to thoroughly evaluate system performance across different architectures of LLMs, we employ several notable models. First, we use the widely recognized GQA-based model Llama-3-8B as introduced by Dubey and colleagues in 2024. Next, we incorporate the MHA-based model Llama-2-7B, as detailed by Touvron and team in 2023. Additionally, we consider the more compact Minitron-4B model developed by Muralidharan and others in 2024. To facilitate long-context inference, we also incorporate the context-enhanced iteration of Llama-3-8B known as Gradient, which was put forward by Pekelis and his team in 2024.

contents.human: Baselines. We consider the following systems as baselines, using their latest versions1 to ensure a fair comparison. Various systems have been developed to enhance LLM deployment efficiency. Orca (Yu et al., 2022) uses iteration-level scheduling and selective batching for distributed systems. vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b) introduces PagedAttention, inspired by virtual memory, to optimize KV cache management. TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) is the industry’s leading solution also featuring inflight batching and PagedAttention inspired by vLLM. LightLLM (Contributors, 2023a) further reduces memory waste in PagedAttention by introducing TokenAttention. SGLang (Zheng et al., 2023) advances LLM programming with a domain-specific language and RadixAttention. LMDeploy (Contributors, 2023b) improves deployment with persistent batching and blocked KV cache. Nanoflow (Zhu et al., 2024) features intra-device scheduling and asynchronous CPU scheduling, while QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) improves LLM serving throughput through W4A8KV4 quantization and system codesign. MLC-LLM (team, 2023) accelerates deployment on edge devices via compiler-based optimizations. Inspired by contextual sparsity (Liu et al., 2023), PowerInfer (Song et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2024b) deploys LLMs on memory-constrained devices via offloading.

contents.human: Sparse Attention. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) reduces attention complexity by blending local, global, and random attention masks. Subsequent methods like StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024) simplify attention patterns by discarding KV caches mid-way through the context. However, these approaches struggle to retain the original models’ long-context capabilities due to limited global context modeling. Recent works like DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2024a), and SeerAttention (Gao et al., 2024) address this issue by introducing retrieval heads (Wu et al., 2024) or combining full attention with local attention heads. Quest (Tang et al., 2024) introduces dynamic, query-aware sparsity for accelerated decoding, while MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) extends similar ideas to the prefilling stage. FastGen (Ge et al., 2023) optimizes decoding by profiling attention heads to discard tokens. PQCache (Zhang et al., 2024a) and ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2024) further advance the selective attention methods with product quantization and low-rank decomposition. Additionally, LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023) finetunes shortcontext LLMs to long-context ones after converting global attention to shifted sparse attention. 7 CONCLUSION We introduce LServe, an efficient serving system for longsequence LLMs that leverages hybrid sparse attention. By incorporating unified block sparse attention, we achieve significant acceleration of the attention mechanism for both LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention 12 prefilling and decoding stages in long-sequence models. We further show that head-level static sparsity and query-aware dynamic sparsity are orthogonal and can be effectively combined with minimal impact on accuracy. LServe surpasses state-of-the-art systems, delivering an average of 1.3×-2.1× speedup in the decoding stage and up to 2.9× speedup in the prefilling stage, preserving the models’ long-context capabilities. contents.AI: Sparse Attention. In the realm of ensuring efficient attention mechanisms, BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) has made strides by integrating local, global, and random attention masks to curtail complexity. Building on this, more recent frameworks such as StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024) have aimed to streamline attention patterns by eliminating KV caches partway through the context process. These methods, however, encounter difficulties in preserving the long-context capabilities inherent to the original models, owing largely to a reduced capacity for global context modeling. Newer endeavors like DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2024a), and SeerAttention (Gao et al., 2024) have tackled this challenge by either incorporating retrieval heads (Wu et al., 2024) or by merging complete attention with localized attention heads. Quest (Tang et al., 2024) offers an innovative approach with a form of dynamic, query-specific sparsity that enhances decoding speed, while MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) applies these concepts to the prefilling stage as well. FastGen (Ge et al., 2023) refines the decoding process by profiling attention heads, allowing for the elimination of tokens. In the vein of selective attention, PQCache (Zhang et al., 2024a) and ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2024) push the frontier further with techniques like product quantization and low-rank decomposition. Furthermore, LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023) fine-tunes short-context Large Language Models (LLMs) to function effectively as long-context models by transforming global attention into shifted sparse attention.7 CONCLUSION We present LServe, an advanced serving system optimized for long-sequence LLMs through the application of hybrid sparse attention. By utilizing a cohesive approach to block sparse attention, this model not only significantly expedites the attention mechanism but does so for both the prefilling and decoding phases in long-sequence models. Our findings reveal that the combination of head-level static sparsity and query-focused dynamic sparsity are complementary approaches that can be combined with negligible accuracy loss. LServe sets itself apart from current leading systems, achieving an average acceleration of 1.3×-2.1× in the decoding stage and up to 2.9× in the prefilling stage, all while maintaining the models’ long-context aptitude.ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS We are grateful for the support from MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab, the MIT AI Hardware Program, the MIT Amazon Science Hub, the National Science Foundation, and Hyundai. Our gratitude also extends to June Yang, Bo Li, and Kaiyu Xie for their insightful discussions.
